newsitem.title: USA: Fur sales in U.S. climbed in 1996, survey says.
newsitem.headline: Fur sales in U.S. climbed in 1996, survey says.

text.p: Fur sales in the United States rose 5 percent in 1996, boosted by cold weather, a healthy economy and apparently waning support for the animal rights movement, the Fur Information Council of America said Tuesday.

Fur sales last year totalled $1.25 billion, up from an estimated $1.2 billion in 1995, according to the annual survey done by Southwick Associates, a research firm, and released by the fur retailers' and manufacturers' organisation.
"The furriers we interviewed reported that consumer interest in fur had definitely increased this year," Rob Southwick, president of the research firm, said in a statement.
Carol Wynne, executive director of the council, also cited "the current shift away from public support of the animal rights movement."
But the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals said its information showed that fur sales have continued to drop.
"Strangling, poisoning and drowning animals for a luxury item is less popular today than it ever was," Lisa Lange, PETA director of public affairs, said.

"It's just absolutely false as far as fur sales being up. You can tell not only by fur sales, but the number of mink farms is down by half and the number of fox farms is down by two-thirds in this country," Lange said.
